summary: Defines version 3 of the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) for IPv4 and IPv6. VRRP elects which router on a LAN is responsible for a virtual router, so another can take over if it fails. It obsoletes RFC 5798, which obsoleted RFC 3768.

eli5.summary: If the main teacher is absent, a substitute steps in so class continues. VRRP lets backup routers take over when the main one fails.

questions: what is the vrrp multicast address
what is the default vrrp priority
subtitle: How backup routers on a LAN agree on who forwards for a shared virtual address, and take over when it fails.

tldr.problem: Hosts on a LAN usually have one default router configured. If it fails, every host that cannot detect another path is cut off.
tldr.mechanism: Several routers share a Virtual Router with its own ID, addresses and MAC address. They elect one Active Router by priority, and only it sends periodic multicast advertisements. If those stop, the best Backup Router takes over.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9568 obsoletes RFC 5798 (which obsoleted RFC 3768). It updates terminology, fixes state machine errata, clarifies the checksum and adds advice on IPv6 and legacy interoperation.

today: RFC 9568 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2024. It obsoletes RFC 5798, which obsoleted RFC 3768, and it is not itself obsoleted or updated by any RFC listed in the metadata.

sections.title: The Problem and What Changed
sections.content:
Many hosts use a single, manually configured default route, for example from a static setting or DHCPv4. That is cheap and widely supported, but it is a single point of failure. The RFC describes the loss of the default router as a catastrophic event that isolates every host unable to detect an alternate path.

VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) is an election protocol that dynamically assigns responsibility for a Virtual Router to one of the VRRP Routers on a LAN. Hosts keep using one address, and the election decides which physical router answers for it. For IPv6, the RFC notes that Neighbor Discovery can take more than 10 seconds to notice a dead router, while a VRRP Backup Router can take over in around three seconds with the default parameters.

This document is version 3 and obsoletes RFC 5798, which in turn obsoleted RFC 3768 (version 2, IPv4 only). Its changes include inclusive terminology (the router in charge is now the Active Router), corrected state machine errata, a clarified checksum, an immediate advertisement when a lower-priority router is heard, and removal of the appendices on FDDI, Token Ring and ATM LAN Emulation. The RFC says VRRP provides a function similar to the proprietary HSRP (RFC 2281).
sections.eli5: If everyone in your street has only one bus to school and it breaks, nobody gets there. VRRP gives the street a spare bus that starts at once, and everyone keeps waiting at the same stop.

sections.title: The Virtual Router Idea
sections.content:
A Virtual Router is defined by a Virtual Router Identifier (VRID, 1 to 255) and a set of either IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. Its scope is a single LAN. The VRID and its addresses must be coordinated among all VRRP Routers on that LAN. The same VRID can be used for an IPv4 set and an IPv6 set, but these are two different Virtual Routers.

The router that owns the protected address as a real interface address is the IP address owner, and it always becomes the Active Router when it is up. Other routers are Backup Routers. Only the Active Router sends periodic advertisements, which keeps traffic low. A Backup Router does not preempt the Active Router unless it has a higher priority, and preemption can be administratively prohibited.

The RFC's second sample network shows two Virtual Routers, where Router-1 is Active for VRID 1 and Backup for VRID 2, and Router-2 the reverse. Hosts split their traffic between the two, giving load-splitting while both are up and full redundancy if one fails. The RFC says the details of load-balancing are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Think of a shared walkie-talkie channel with a name. Whoever is the captain answers on it, and if the captain goes quiet, the next person in line picks up.

sections.title: The Advertisement Packet
sections.content:
VRRP has a single packet type, ADVERTISEMENT (type 1), sent in an IPv4 or IPv6 packet to a link-local multicast group. IPv4 uses 224.0.0.18 and IPv6 uses ff02:0:0:0:0:0:0:12. The IP protocol number or Next Header is 112. Routers MUST NOT forward datagrams with those destinations.

The IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit MUST be 255, and a receiver MUST discard a packet where it is not. This protects against advertisements injected from another network.

After the IP header come the Version (3), Type, Virtual Rtr ID, Priority and IPvX Addr Count fields, then a 4-bit Reserve (zero on send, ignored on receipt), a 12-bit Max Advertise Interval in centiseconds (default 100, which is 1 second), a 16-bit checksum and the list of addresses. An address count of 0 means the advertisement MUST be ignored. For IPv6, the first address MUST be the link-local address of the Virtual Router. The addresses exist for troubleshooting misconfigured routers.

The checksum is the usual one's complement checksum over the VRRP message. For IPv4 it does not include a pseudo-header. For IPv6 it does, with Next Header 112.
sections.eli5: The packet is a short note from the captain: who I am, how important I am, and how often I will say hello. It is shouted to everyone in the room, never sent outside it.

sections.title: Priority and Failover Timing
sections.content:
Priority is an 8-bit number where higher wins. The address owner uses 255. Routers backing up a Virtual Router MUST use 1 to 254, and the default is 100. A priority of 0 is special: the Active Router is saying it has stopped participating, so Backup Routers can take over without waiting out the timer.

A Backup Router declares the Active Router down after Active_Down_Interval, calculated as (3 * Active_Adver_Interval) + Skew_Time. The skew is ((256 - Priority) * Active_Adver_Interval) / 256, so higher-priority Backup Routers wait slightly less and tend to win. The RFC says election convergence takes less than 4 seconds with the default interval and can be configured to under 1/25 second.

Two other settings matter. Preempt_Mode (default True) controls whether a higher-priority router takes over from a lower-priority Active Router, except that the address owner always preempts. Accept_Mode (default False) controls whether an Active Router that is not the address owner accepts packets addressed to the owner's address, for example pings.

The RFC recommends giving routers different priorities with sufficient gaps, so two Backup Routers do not both become Active at once. It also notes that a very small advertisement interval combined with queueing delay can cause routers to flap, and suggests giving VRRP packets priority on egress queues.
sections.eli5: Everyone gets a number for how much they should be in charge. If the captain stays silent for about three hellos, the highest number steps up a little sooner than the others.

sections.title: The State Machine
sections.content:
Each VRRP Router runs one state machine per Virtual Router, with three states: Initialize, Backup and Active. In Initialize the router waits for a Startup event. If its priority is 255 it sends an advertisement, announces its addresses (a gratuitous ARP for IPv4, an unsolicited Neighbor Advertisement for IPv6) and goes to Active. Otherwise it starts the Active_Down_Timer and goes to Backup.

In Backup, the router must not answer ARP requests or Neighbor Solicitations for the Virtual Router addresses, must not send Router Advertisements, and must discard packets sent to the Virtual Router MAC address. When the Active_Down_Timer fires, it sends an advertisement, announces the addresses with the Virtual Router MAC and becomes Active. A received priority 0 advertisement shortens the timer to Skew_Time.

In Active, the router answers ARP and ND requests, forwards packets sent to the Virtual Router MAC address, and sends periodic advertisements. If it hears a higher-priority advertisement (or an equal priority with a higher primary IP address), it drops to Backup. If it hears a lower priority one, it discards it and immediately sends its own advertisement, so learning bridges update. On a Shutdown event it sends an advertisement with priority 0 and returns to Initialize.
sections.eli5: A router is either waiting to start, standing by as the substitute, or being the one in charge. It changes jobs only when the boss goes quiet or someone more important shows up.

sections.title: Virtual MAC, ARP and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
Hosts must keep using the same MAC address after a failover. So the Virtual Router MAC address is 00-00-5E-00-01-{VRID} for IPv4 and 00-00-5E-00-02-{VRID} for IPv6. The Active Router MUST answer ARP requests and ND Neighbor Solicitations with that address, never its physical one, and it sends advertisements from the Virtual Router MAC so learning bridges find the right LAN segment.

At boot, ARP and ND messages MUST be delayed until both the address and the Virtual Router MAC are configured. For IPv6, the RFC advises that Backup Routers send the same Router Advertisement options as the address owner. It also says a Virtual Router MAC MUST NOT be used for deriving IPv6 interface identifiers, and that Active and Backup Routers SHOULD accept Unsolicited Neighbor Advertisements.

A non-owner Active Router SHOULD NOT forward packets addressed to the Virtual Router address, since that creates useless traffic and possible loops. One method is to install a host Drop Route when it becomes Active. ICMP redirects work normally, and proxy ARP must also use the Virtual Router MAC.
sections.eli5: Everyone writes to the same mailbox name, no matter which substitute is working that day. The mailbox name belongs to the job, not the person.

sections.title: Working With VRRPv2
sections.content:
Interoperation between VRRPv2 and VRRPv3 is optional and intended only for upgrades; it is NOT RECOMMENDED for permanent deployments. An implementation MAY have a flag to send and listen for both versions. An Active Router in this mode MUST send both at the configured rate, and a Backup Router times out based on the Active Router's rate, converting VRRPv2 seconds to centiseconds.

Two cautions are given. A VRRPv2 router should not have a higher priority than a router using a sub-second rate. Also, a VRRPv3 Active Router sending at centisecond rates might overwhelm a VRRPv2 Backup, so deployments should start at a slower rate such as 100 centiseconds until the VRRPv2 routers are upgraded.
sections.eli5: When a team switches to a new walkie-talkie, the old and new ones can talk for a while. But the old ones should go in the bin once everyone has switched.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
VRRP for IPvX does not include authentication. Earlier versions had several types, but operational experience found that misconfigured secrets caused multiple Active Routers to be elected. The RFC also argues that cryptographic protection would not stop a hostile node from acting as an Active Router, and a hostile LAN node can disrupt ARP and ND anyway.

The RFC says these attacks are a subset of what any node on a LAN can already do. The TTL and Hop Limit of 255 check limits most problems to the local network. Some L2 switches can filter VRRP from ports with end-hosts. VRRP provides no confidentiality, and none is needed. If SEND is deployed, VRRP is compatible with it, provided Active and Backup Routers share the prefix delegation but keep their own key pairs.
sections.eli5: Anyone standing in the room could pretend to be captain, so the rule is that notes only count if they come from inside the room.

fields.name: Priority
fields.desc: 255 for the address owner, 1 to 254 for backups, 0 when stepping down.

fields.name: Reserve
fields.desc: Zero on send, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement checksum of the VRRP message.
